content.text: To test an English argument, first ask whether it seems valid. Then translate it and run the star test. If the two answers differ, check your work.
Use the same letter for the same idea and different letters for different ideas. A name, or a phrase with 'the' that picks out one thing, gets a small letter.

examples.title: A general term: invalid
lines: Al is a man. (a is M)
My father is a man. (f is M)
examples.conclusion: So Al is my father. (a* is f*)
examples.note: M is not starred, so the test fails. Many people are men, so Al and my father can differ.

examples.title: A singular term: valid
lines: Al is the mayor. (a is m)
My father is the mayor. (f is m)
examples.conclusion: So Al is my father. (a* is f*)
examples.note: There is no capital letter, and one star falls after is. The mayor is one person, so both are that person.

examples.title: Martin Luther King's argument
lines: All segregation laws degrade human personality. (all S* is D)
All laws that degrade human personality are unjust. (all D* is U)
examples.conclusion: So all segregation laws are unjust. (all S is U*)
examples.note: Each capital is starred once and one star falls after is. Valid.

question.prompt: How should 'the president' be written in an argument?
options: A capital letter, as a general term
A small letter, as one person
question.hint: Does 'the president' name a kind of thing, or one particular person?
question.explanation: 'The president' picks out one person, so it gets a small letter. 'Presidents' would be a general term with a capital.
